 Filing58198 generation firming requirement

I am usingthis filingto emphasis to the Commission the need for a market design to
replace the PCM not just a firming requirement as per statute. But my comments are
relevant to the statute as well. Firming meant something else to an old utility engineer. A
firm system wasonethat had enough generation capabilityplus reserves, and everyone
understood their responsibility to firm up their load.

Firmingnow should mean that enough dispatchable generation is installed system wideto
meet the ERCOT Reliability Standard. This may be a new concept to some that read this,
and it is part of my market design that I have submitted to the legislature and more recently
tothe PUCChairman.

The ERCOT grid cannot be firmed without buildingthe necessary gas fired power plants.
And of course, they need to perform during scarcity periods as contemplated bythis
project. But they need to be built first.

Each load serving entity has a firming obligation to supply their load with a proportionate
share in and pay for the cost of the needed dispatchable generation. If not, who else has
such obligation?And each LSE can purchasetheirallocated share using powerand energy
contracts in the bilateral market in use today. The obligation applies to Municipal and
Cooperative utilities as well. These contracts are used now and have been used for many
years by the transmission dependent utilities in the bilateral market.

The PCM was brilliantly conceived but was endlessly complicated and it needs to be
replaced with a market design that will get the necessary dispatchable plants built for
reliability. That is how the system needs to be "firmed" whether that is intended bythis
project or not. There is a much simpler way to determine the needed dispatchable
generation capability system wide and for each load serving entity which will be described
below.

The reliability standard.

The ERCOT consultant E3 calculated the need for 13GW of generation to meet the 0.1 days
peryear reliability standard and determined that today's energy only market system has a
3.2 days peryear loss of load probability. (see ERCOT workshop Apr 17,2024, E3 power
point slide 12). E3 said when questioned at that meeting by me, that their computer model
can be usedto calculate the needed dispatchable generation in GW to meetthe reliability
standard inthe future. Their model looks at many factors includinghistorical weather
patterns, various shortage periods, forced outage rates of fossil and renewables etc... In
other words, to get backto an earlier point, allthe complexitythatthe questionsthis
 project is asking are taken care of bythe computer model. The reliability standard using
the E3 model can determine how much installed dispatchable generation is needed now,
and in the future, to achieve a reliable system.

Proven generation capability: Capabilitytests have been the norm for many years for
turbine driven dispatchable generation to prove availability.

Penalties: Penalties are not needed for lack of operational availability for legitimate
reasons. Penalties are not necessaryto keep people "honest", andtheydrive up costs to
the public. They should only be used forthose rare cases where violations become
evident.

Verification: ERCOT should verify each year that each LSE has firmed their load with the
necessarycontractpurchases of dispatchable generation. Considerapplyingan
adjustment utilizinga residual auction to determine pricing.

Gaming the system: Withholding generation to drive up prices will not work, and the
incentive to do so will be removed if the scarcity pricing model is replaced with my
reliability model described above.

Market power: The large generation companies cannot dominate the market but rather the
opposite effect will occur with my market design. Once the amount of new generation is
determined bythe reliability standard (see above)thegeneratingcompaniesthat attempt
to price gouge will be left behind. It is called competition. But we still have IMM and OPUC
lookingover everyone's shoulderand of course we havethe justice department.

Allocation of the total dispatchable generation to each LSE: Each LSE has an obligation
to acquire power and energy from a dispatchable generation plant or plants to firm up their
load, and that can be accomplished by allocation of the total requirement for such
generation to each LSE in proportion to the size of their firm load. This is not optional as it is
now. Some hedge and some don't, but everyone should for a level playing field for
competition. Everyone paystheir fair share of the cost of dispatchable generation.

Net energy for load during scarcity periods should NOT be used to allocate because it will
varywidely among LSEs and places a disproportionate economic benefitto those that have
more renewables than others and introduces a variabilitythat makes this approach
complicated, difficultto calculate, practicallyimpossibleto forecast, and is not fairto all
concerned.

Allocation of the dispatchable generation obligation is applied to all LSEs to achieve a level
playing field for competition. There is no need to limit renewables or demand side options
afterthe reliability obligation is met.
 My preference is to use metered sales as an allocator. Metered sales is the common
quantity for every LSE and can indicate the relative size of each. The less sales the LSE has
the less their load is of the total and the less their obligation to pay for plants. Or vise versa.
Think about using before rejectingthe suggestion. Native energy for load might be another
alternative. But never net load after subtracting renewables. No no no.

Build the plants, save money, and improve the environment the E3 study mentioned
earlier shows an average annual savings of $5.9 billion peryear in operating costs. This is
more than enough savings to finance the needed 13GW with savings that can be passed
through to the electric customers. Buildingthe plants will save money and improve the
environment because the newer plants displace the older more expensive and dirtier
plants in day-to-day operation. But to achieve the savings there must be a change in the
market design forthe generation companies to collectthe needed revenue to build them.

Do the math. The plants pay for themselves in less than 5 years. There is net savings after
subtractingthe annual carrying charges. That savings can result in lower wholesale costs
that can be passed through to the ultimate consumer. But there must be a willingness to
fund the plants that doesn't exist now. Pay money to save money.

Executive Summary

Each LSE has an obligation to firm their load.

First: The system wide need for dispatchable generation is determined by the reliability
standard and is updated as needed. Second: Each LSE will be allocated their fair share of
thetotaldispatchable generation requirement based on the proportion each LSEs load is
to the total system load. Finally: Each LSE can contract fortheir share of the total
dispatchable generation by usingindividual powerand energy contacts thatare used today
in the bilateral market, and that have been used by transmission dependent utilities for
manyyears. Itisthat simple.

What has just been described is a Reliability Market Model (myterm for my plan) that will
ensure that the reliability of the system is protected without limiting renewables and
demand side options. It is easyto implement, enhances competition, and will result in a
limited butadequate supply of dispatchable generation. Competition among LSEswill
result in lower prices to the ultimate consumer. The generation companies will build
because they know all LSEs will paytheir costs to build the plants in the bilateral market.
Buildingthe generation will save electric customers money and improve the environment.

Thomas L Dane,

Retired engineer, utility manager, and former ERCOT board member
